diagnosis.title: Incorrect compaction
diagnosis.summary: The compaction prompt or algorithm drops information that later work still needs, so the agent repeats work, misses a requirement, or asks for permission again.

definition.p: Compaction makes room by forgetting most of a conversation. It has to predict what will matter next: keep the decisions, constraints, permissions, and findings needed for unfinished work, and discard irrelevant history. This diagnosis proposes that the compactor is making that choice badly.

For example, it may preserve a long account of completed edits but drop the user’s instruction to leave a particular file alone. The agent then resumes without that restriction. The same visible mistake has a different explanation if the restriction survived in the context.

intervention-ref.when: A compaction summary has lost important information, and you can change the compaction prompt or algorithm.

expected-improvement.p: After compaction, the agent should reread fewer unchanged sources, follow the saved requirements, and stop asking again for permission already given.

still-necessary.p: It should check sources that may have changed and ask permission for work outside the original scope. The summary should still discard irrelevant history.

reason-to-reconsider.p: If the important information survives but the same mistakes continue, investigate how the agent uses it. Problems that start before compaction need another explanation.

possible-harm.p: Keeping too much can crowd out useful context. Keeping a permission but losing its limits can lead to unauthorized work.

criterion.title: The information mattered
criterion.p: Identify a fact, requirement, or permission that was in the conversation before compaction and was needed afterward.

criterion.title: Compaction dropped it
criterion.p: The summary or the model’s context after compaction omits or changes that information. If you cannot inspect either, keep information loss as a hypothesis.

criterion.title: The omission explains the mistake
criterion.p: The next work shows repeated retrieval, breaks the missing requirement, or asks for the lost permission. Show which missing fact would have helped; timing alone is not enough.

exclusion.title: Information no longer needed
exclusion.p: Forgetting is useful when a fact is obsolete, a task is finished, or permission has expired. Keeping everything would defeat compaction.

exclusion.title: The meaning survived
exclusion.p: A shorter wording may preserve the same meaning. If the relevant information is still clear, there may be a problem with following it, but it was not lost during compaction.

alternative.title: The agent never had the information

discriminator.p: Check the conversation before compaction. A fact in an unread file was never available to summarize; improve how the agent finds or records it.

alternative.title: Another instruction demands the repeated work

discriminator.p: If the summary retains a passed test but a standing rule requires another run anyway, changing compaction will not remove that rule. Consider overbroad verification instructions.

alternative.title: The agent has the information but does not use it

discriminator.p: If the needed fact is clear in the current context, look for conflicting instructions or a failure to follow it. Rewriting the summary may not help.

investigation.p: Compare the conversation just before compaction with its summary and the next mistake. Look for something the compactor discarded that the unfinished task was likely to need, and for less useful material it kept instead.
